PCI.BIO: Erik Chumacero is an Assistant Professor since Sep/19. Prior to join UTRGV, he got a PhD degree on Mechanical Engineering from Texas Tech University (Lubbock, Texas) and another PhD on Physics from Paris Sud University (Paris, France). His research interests include robotics, mechatronics, system dynamics and control, and biomechanics.

CONGRANT.TITLE: REU Site: Hands-On Undergraduate Research to Advancing Agricultural Robotics in the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.CONTENT_GOAL: GOAL 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The overarching goal of this REU-site is to recruit and train talented undergraduates by immersing them in meaningful, hands-on research experiences that build technical expertise, enhance problem-solving skills, and prepare them for graduate studies and STEM careers. Central to this goal is engaging students in core robotics research areas—motion planning, sensor integration, control, localization, and human-robot interaction—while grounding these efforts in the specific needs and operational constraints of the RGV region. The program prioritizes the development of transferable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, and communication, recognizing that these outcomes are the most enduring benefits of research participation. While groundbreaking discoveries are welcomed, the program's true mission is to equip students with the knowledge, mindset, and abilities needed for advanced study and impactful STEM careers.

The proposed REU-site seeks support for three annual summer cohorts of undergraduate students. Each year, ten students will join UTRGV for a ten-week immersive, research-focused experience in which the design and mock field-testing of robotic systems naturally immerse students in core robotics research topics while supporting broader exploration beyond the prototypes themselves. REU participants will work collaboratively in interdisciplinary teams and alongside UTRGV's graduate student population.

Through this structure, the program aims to achieve the following objectives:

Intellectual Focus: To conduct research in robotics aimed at advancing motion planning, sensor integration, control, and human-robot collaboration for systems intended to operate under the environmental conditions and operational constraints commonly found in rural and agricultural regions of the RGV.

Educational Objective: To provide research opportunities for undergraduates—particularly those from the RGV, enabling them to contribute to solving regionally relevant engineering challenges while deepening their engagement through hands-on projects that connect directly to local agricultural and rural needs.

CONGRANT.TITLE: R-LAB (Robotics Lab in a Phone) - Introducing underrepresented students to STEM career pathways through Robotics in an Informal Setting
R-LAB(Robotics Lab in a Phone) - Introducing underrepresented students to STEM career pathways through Robotics in an Informal Setting
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
This pilots and feasibility studies AISL project aims to provide a quality STEM learning experience by providing opportunities to middle school and high school students to get exposed to the basics of engineering (i.e., in electronics, robotics, programming, and applied mathematics) at the intersection of Mobile-based learning and Robotics. The primary goal of this project is to develop an effective mechanism for underrepresented and low-income middle school and high school students to stimulate their participation and increase their awareness in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM). At the core of this project, we propose to design and develop a pilot robotic kit that consists of a 3D-printed robotic arm manipulator with an integrated mobile-based application (R-LAB) to guide students to first build and later program the robotic arm manipulator. This robotic kit is aimed to provide students with an informal learning experience with minimal supervision. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include (1) Designing and developing pilot robotic kits to be distributed among 75 middle and high school students from the Brownsville Independent School District (BISD). Each kit will be composed of a 3D printable robotic arm manipulator and a mobile-based smartphone application that will guide students in building and programming the robotic arm; (2) Organizing virtual and in-person family café sessions where STEM industry and academic speakers will be invited to interact with students and their parents in order to promote STEM professions; and (3) Conducting guided virtual and in-person industry tours to local industries in the Rio Grande Valley to provide students with a real-life approach to what engineering is.

Guided by an integrated STEM learning framework tailored for informal learning, this project aims to demystify the field of engineering and encourage students to reevaluate career choices and pursue a STEM profession. In addition, by using the proposed R-LAB smart-phone application, students will have opportunities to explore engineering and coding in an informal context.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Advancing Manufacturing Capabilities - Exploring the application of Drones for Material Handling and Quality Control in Manufacturing Industries
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The evolution of industrial systems toward Industry 4.0 depends on the interconnectivity of products and processes throughout the whole manufacturing life cycle. Industry 4.0; characterized by emerging technologies of advanced data analytics, robotics, and automation; has a huge potential to reshape the manufacturing industry in several domains within the next 5 to 10 years. This shift in manufacturing production systems is influencing the demand for the use and integration of autonomous systems in manufacturing production. Towards addressing this need, the primary goal of this project is to explore the application of unmanned aerial vehicles, commonly known as drones, in manufacturing to automate Quality Control processes and Material Handling tasks in highly complex environments such as factories, storage facilities, and warehouses. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include: (A) Engaging with subject matter experts and professionals from manufacturing industries to explore and identify opportunities and challenges for integrating drones in manufacturing, (B) Develop an interactive drone-based online quality control system for product and process inspection to be deployed and tested using applied use cases in manufacturing industries, and (C) To explore the application and logistics of drone-drone co-operative manipulation (DDCM) and human-drone co-operative manipulation (HDCM) in manufacturing industries through computational modeling, simulations, and prototypes. This project successfully executed has the potential to substantially advance the state-of-the-art quality control processes and logistics in future manufacturing through a novelty harvesting of the potential of robotic-drone platforms.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Engaged student learning in Robotics and Automation for  Green and Agricultural Systems Design
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is seeking to increase the number of Hispanic and low-income students attaining skills in agricultural robotics and automation set through continued engaged student learning. To reflect the project goal of training future workforce and augmenting their interest towards applied robotics and automation technology in agriculture and production, project objectives include (a) Establish a tailored educational community to train and prepare students with skills relevant to modern agricultural techniques, (b) Develop new course modules  to be integrated with current curricula at UTRGV to improve student technical workforce readiness levels on emerging agricultural technologies and, (c) Provide experiential learning opportunities to students via hands-on applied research projects. This project supported by its design addresses the significant factors, which influence the retention of Hispanic students in STEM based curricula. The hybrid approach in identifying activities that overlap student curricula and the proposed student support system will improve student learning experience along with introducing them to emerging technology trends. This project will ultimately establish a platform for increasing the retention of students in STEM.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Engineering for All: Engaging High School Students on STEM Fields Through Robotics Summer Workshops
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
In assuring the Halliburton’s core values, the Manufacturing and Industrial Engineering Department at
the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), in collaboration with Brownsville Independent
School District (BISD), propose to organize a 5-week Summer workshop on Robotics tailored for
engaging high school students in College STEM education and improving students’ skills in Robotics,
Additive Manufacturing, and Programming, which are critical in many modern industries (such as oil and
gas). We will especially encourage students from under-represented minorities such as females and
Hispanics to participate. A total of 35 students will be invited from different BISD high schools to
participate in the proposed workshop, where they will design and develop a 3D printed robotic arm. The
main objectives of this effort are to: (a) Provide a structured hands-on experience in the fields of
Computer Aided Design, 3D printing, robotics, programming, and control, key features of the modern
and future industry, (b) Stimulate student technical skills by teaching them basic programming skills on
Arduino Microcontroller, (c) Create a competitive atmosphere and encourage students give their best
effort in a team environment, (d) Increase community engagement and promote enrollment in STEM
programs, (e) Increase visibility of Halliburton in the Rio Grande Valley during the proposed workshop by
providing information on the role of Halliburton in oil and gas industry along with the available career
opportunities in STEM fields that Halliburton offers.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Enhancing Engineering and Technology Career Pathways: Recruiting, Retaining, and Graduating Underrepresented Students in the Era of Digital Transformation
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), a major Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI)
located in the border region of United States and Mexico is seeking to increase participation, retention
and graduation rates among minority low-income students in the critically needed engineering and
technology programs. This project provides innovative ways for adapting effective evidence based
curricular and co-curricular activities aimed to improve undergraduate student academic success. The
primary goal of this project is to encourage and increase the number of students towards obtaining their
degrees in STEM by providing 30 undergradaute students with four-year scholarships, and 17
undergraduate students with two-year scholarships (47 total), spread across four cohorts. In addition, we
emphasize on improved student technical workforce readiness levels by establishing an academic support
system at the College of Engineering and Computer Science (COECS) to encourage students to pursue
careers in emerging fields of engineering and technology.
Building on existing student support services at UTRGV, this project includes technical and academic
success workshops, professional development, peer mentoring, industry certifications and internships, and
developing course modules integrated with Engineering Technology and Manufacturing Engineering
curriculum. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include: (a) To increase student
enrollment of Manufacturing and Engineering Technology undergraduate programs created to train and
prepare students with high-tech skills in the fields of manufacturing, automation and systems engineering;
(b) Developing an Eco-System in COECS with tailored student centric activities to address student’s precollege
experience, social-cultural experience, institutional experience, and college experience
specifically targeting underrepresented demographics; (c) Financially support undergraduate students by
awarding S-STEM scholarships over the grant period; and (d) Build partnerships with industry to provide
more learning and internship opportunities for students.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: THE EFFECT OF THE BALANCE BOARD MASS ON THE STABILITY, EQUILIBRIUM, AND  ROBUSTNESS OF THE HUMAN-BALANCE BOARD SYSTEM
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Design Engineering Technical Conferences  and Computers and Information in Engineering Conference
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: People  with  neuromuscular  deficits  may  show  balance  issues that  put  them  in  high  risk  of  fall.  To  reduce  the  risk,  balance-board  (BB)  based  training  has  been  widely  used.  However, despite the extensive use of BB-based training, the mechanisms responsible  for  rehabilitation  remain  unclear.  To  fill  this  gap; several  studies  have  used  a  system  dynamics  approach  to investigate  the  effect  of  neuromuscular  deficits  (visual, vestibular,  proprioceptive)  and  sensorimotor  latencies  on  the stability  and  dynamical  behavior  of  the  human-BB  system. Though,  to the  best  knowledge of  the authors,  the effect  of the BB mass on the stability and dynamics of the human-BB system has  never  been  investigated.  In  the  present  study,  bifurcation analyses, root finding techniques, and simulation are applied to investigate the effect of the BB mass and BB time-delay on the stability,  equilibrium,  and robustness  of  the  human-BB  upright posture (UP) for cases where either proprioceptive or visual and vestibular  deficits  are  simulated.  The  results  show  that  the  BB mass  and  time-delay  play  a  critical  role  on  the  UP  stability, leaning  postures,  and  robustness  of  the  human-BB  system.  In fact,  increasing  BB  mass  reduces  the  range  of  neuromuscular gains that stabilize the system and shrinks the basin of attraction of  the  UP,  which  is  related  to  the  robustness  to  disturbances. This  effect  is  more  evident  in  the  case  where  visual  and vestibular  deficits  are  simulated.  This  relationship  has implications on the design and development of BBs with tunable mass  and  time-delay.  The  BB  could  be  designed  to  tune  time-delay  and  mass,  so  patients  could  be  challenged  during  BB training in a more patient-specific manner.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Direct Torque Control of Electric Current Phase and Frequency in the Permanent-Magnet Synchronous  Generator
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Design Engineering Technical Conferences and   Computers and Information in Engineering Conference
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The  control  design,  formal  stability  analysis,  and  simulation results of a direct-torque controller applied to the permanent magnet synchronous generator (PMSG) is presented here. The controlled  variables  are  the  PMSG’s  phase,  amplitude,  and frequency of the alternating current (AC) signal. For control design  purposes  and  computer  simulation,  the  PMSG  is modeled in the    frame of reference. On the other hand, the control algorithm is designed via backstepping technique and Lyapunov  asymptotic  stability  is  demonstrated  for  tracking error  of  the  mechanical  velocity  and  the  electrical  current. Uniform asymptotic stability is proved in a twofold procedure. First,  it  is  shown  that  both  mechanical  and  electrical subsystems of the PMSG are input to state stable with respect to  conveniently  selected  inputs.  Second,  uniform  asymptotic stability  of  the  interconnected  mechanical  and  electrical subsystems  is  shown  via  Lyapunov’s  stability  direct  method. Finally, the performance of the closed-loop  system, composed of  the  PMSG  model  and  the  control  algorithm,  is  tested  via numerical simulations, which show that the three-phase electric currents in the PMSG and the rotor’s mechanical  velocity track the imposed reference signals.

PRESENT.TITLE: THE EFFECT OF THE BALANCE BOARD MASS ON THE STABILITY, EQUILIBRIUM, AND ROBUSTNESS  OF THE HUMAN-BALANCE BOARD SYSTEM
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: <sup>People  with  neuromuscular  deficits  may  show  balance  issues that  put  them  in  high  risk  of  fall.  To  reduce  the  risk,  balance-board  (BB)-based  rehabilitation  intervention  has  been  widely used.  However,  despite  the  extensive  use  of  BB-based interventions,  the  mechanisms  responsible  for  rehabilitation remain unclear. To better understand these mechanisms; several studies have used a system dynamics approach to investigate the effect  of  neuromuscular  deficits  (visual,  vestibular,  proprio-ceptive)  and  sensorimotor  latencies  on  the  stability  and dynamical behavior of the human-BB system. Though, to the best knowledge  of  the  authors,  the  effect  of  the  BB  mass  on  the stability and dynamics of the human-BB system has never been investigated.  In  the  present  study,  bifurcation  analyses,  root finding  techniques,  and  computational  simulations  are  used  to investigate the effect of the BB mass and BB time-delay on the stability,  equilibrium,  and robustness  of  the  human-BB  upright posture (UP) for cases where either proprioceptive or visual and vestibular deficits are considered in simulation. The results show that the BB mass and time-delay play a critical role on the UP stability,  leaning  postures,  and  robustness  of  the  human-BB system.  In  fact,  increasing  BB  mass  reduces  the  range  of neuromuscular  gains  that  stabilize  the  system  and  shrinks  the basin of attraction of the UP, which is related to the human-BB system’s robustness to posture disturbances. This effect is more evident  in  the  case  where  visual  and  vestibular  deficits  are considered  in  simulation.  This  relationship  may  have implications on the design and development of BBs with tunable mass and tunable time-delay. The BB could be designed to tune time-delay  and  mas,  so  patients  could  be  better  challenged</sup>
